\section*{Question 5}

Consider the differential equation \(\frac{d y}{d x}=5 x^{2}-\frac{6}{y-2}\) for \(y \neq 2\). Let \(y=f(x)\) be the particular solution to this differential equation with the initial condition \(f(-1)=-4\).
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] Evaluate \(\frac{d y}{d x}\) and \(\frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}\) at (-1, -4).
\item[(b)] Is it possible for the \(x\)-axis to be tangent to the graph of \(f\) at some point? Explain why or why not.
\item[(c)] Find the second-degree Taylor polynomial for \(f\) about \(x=-1\).
\item[(d)] Use Euler's method, starting at \(x=-1\) with two steps of equal size, to approximate \(f(0)\). Show the work that leads to your answer.
\item[(a)] \(\left.\frac{d y}{d x}\right|_{(-1,-4)}=6\)
\[
\frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}=10 x+6(y-2)^{-2} \frac{d y}{d x}
\]
\[
\left.\frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}\right|_{(-1,-4)}=-10+6 \frac{1}{(-6)^{2}} 6=-9
\]
\item[(b)] The \(x\)-axis will be tangent to the graph of \(f\) if \(\left.\frac{d y}{d x}\right|_{(k, 0)}=0\). The \(x\)-axis will never be tangent to the graph of \(f\) because \(\left.\frac{d y}{d x}\right|_{(k, 0)}=5 k^{2}+3>0\) for all \(k\).
\item[(c)] \(P(x)=-4+6(x+1)-\frac{9}{2}(x+1)^{2}\)
\item[(d)] \(f(-1)=-4\)
\[
\begin{aligned}
& f\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) \approx-4+\frac{1}{2}(6)=-1 \\
& f(0) \approx-1+\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{5}{4}+2\right)=\frac{5}{8}
\end{aligned}
\]
\item[] \(3:\left\{\begin{array}{l}1:\left.\frac{d y}{d x}\right|_{(-1,-4)} \\ 1: \frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}} \\ 1:\left.\frac{d^{2} y}{d x^{2}}\right|_{(-1,-4)}\end{array}\right.\)
\item[] \(2:\left\{\begin{array}{l}1: \frac{d y}{d x}=0 \text { and } y=0 \\ 1: \text { answer and explanation }\end{array}\right.\)
\item[] \(2:\left\{\begin{array}{l}1: \text { quadratic and centered at } x=-1 \\ 1: \text { coefficients }\end{array}\right.\)
\item[2] : \(\left\{\begin{array}{l}1: \text { Euler's method with } 2 \text { steps } \\ 1: \text { Euler's approximation to } f(0)\end{array}\right.\)
\end{itemize}
